caption:
A federal judge in California says Claude subscribers can keep pressing their claims that Anthropic oversold its Max plans.
Anthropic promised "5x or 20x more usage" than Pro, but the plaintiffs say weekly limits leave the $200 plan at about 6 times Pro.
The judge kept the negligent misrepresentation and breach of contract claims and dismissed others.

paragraphs.text: Anthropic must face part of a proposed class action claiming it overstated how much usage its Claude Max subscriptions provide, according to a report by The Next Web based on Courthouse News. Magistrate Judge Alex Tse of the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California issued the ruling on Friday, November 6, 2026.

The case, Kahn v. Anthropic, was filed in June 2026 by Karl Kahn, and a related complaint was later brought by Solomon Smith. It covers the Max plans Anthropic sells for $100 and $200 a month alongside its $20 Pro plan.

Anthropic marketed the two Max tiers as offering "5x or 20x more usage than the Pro plan." The plaintiffs argue that the multiplier applies only to the session limit, which resets every five hours, while weekly limits that Anthropic introduced in August 2025 also apply to Max subscribers and are not 5 or 20 times higher.

Using their own calculations for one Claude model, the plaintiffs say the $200 plan delivers about six times Pro's weekly usage and the $100 plan about 3.5 times. The original complaint put the range for the top plan at six to eight times Pro and said the actual usage of both Max plans is far below what was advertised.

Earlier coverage noted that Anthropic's Max support page does list the limits. A viral Reddit post cited by Engadget in September calculated that, once the weekly cap is counted, the $200 plan offered about 1.7 times the usage of the $100 plan despite costing twice as much.

Judge Tse allowed the negligent misrepresentation and breach of contract claims to proceed, along with Smith's claim under a state consumer protection law. He dismissed the claims brought under California's laws on unfair business practices and false advertising, dismissed Kahn's state consumer law claim with room to add detail, and rejected the argument that Anthropic acted unfairly by tightening usage limits during billing periods.

Anthropic had argued that customers should understand the extra usage as a per session figure and pointed to a help page that explains this. The judge rejected that argument, writing that the per session disclosure was located two hyperlinks away from the main sales pages on claude.com. Because subscribers pay monthly, he found they could reasonably read the promise as applying to each month, according to the report.

Anthropic and the plaintiffs did not immediately respond to requests for comment from Courthouse News, The Next Web reported. The Next Web also said it had not reviewed the ruling itself. Anthropic renamed its Max plans the week before the ruling.

The ruling does not decide whether Anthropic misled anyone. It only means the core contract and misrepresentation theories survive the first test. Still, the judge's focus on where the limits were disclosed puts pressure on a common practice among AI companies, which sell plans with multipliers and rolling caps that are hard for buyers to compare. Usage limits have become one of the main points of friction between AI labs and their heaviest paying users.

The next step to watch is whether Kahn files an amended complaint and whether the court certifies a class covering everyone who bought a Max plan since April 2025, which would raise the financial stakes for Anthropic.
